🇷🇺🇨🇳⚛️➡️🌍💸 | The World Bank Just ABANDONED Its 45-Year Anti-Nuclear Power Policy

For decades, the World Bank has been an enforcement arm for the U.S. and Wall Street-led “rules-based” economic order. Its shocking reversal on financing nuclear energy projects is a sign of the West being dragged, kicking and screaming, by China and Russia into a shifting paradigm for development.

After pouring tens of billions of dollars into “least-cost” climate strategies that shackled much of the developing world to unreliable renewable energies like solar and wind, the World Bank is taking a small step forward to Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s original 1944 vision. 

In proposing a post-World War 2 International Bank for Reconstruction & Development, FDR called for a bank that would mass-produce prosperity exactly the way TVA’s turbines electrified the rural South: long-term public credit, mega-engineering projects, cheap power, higher wages, and peace through development. 

He was aware of the peaceful potential of atomic energy, thanks to briefings from American scientist Vannevar Bush.

But at the 1944 Bretton Woods Conference, the British delegation, led by the beastly John Maynard Keynes, smuggled in an austerity Trojan Horse: global monetary “discipline” first, industrial take-off later. 

The only nuclear power project funded by the World Bank was a small reactor in Latina, Italy in 1959, a pathetic drop in the bucket compared to the bank’s potential. The Bank also funded some hydro mega-projects giants like India’s Bhakra-Nangal and Ghana’s Akosombo, which were at the scale FDR pictured.

But after Keynes laid the groundwork, his nefarious and direct disciple E.F. Schumacher delivered the killshot when his Small is Beautiful philosophy was embraced by World Bank head Robert McNamara in 1973. 
Instead of helping developing nations leap-frog into high-energy modernity, the World Bank would focus on: - "Appropriate technologies” 
- At the “least cost” 

The result?  Subsistence and dependence on imports were incentivized. Instead of sovereignty through internal improvements.

McNamara’s direction was followed by a 1975 report titled “Nuclear Power: Its Significance for the Developing World.” It set such demanding safeguards (spent-fuel take-back, accident liability, vendor guarantees) that the World Bank stopped preparing nuclear loans altogether.

In Indonesia and the Philippines, World Bank economists ruled nuclear “uneconomic,” steering governments into gas, coal and geothermal developments with a shorter leash. In 1989, the bank teamed up with the National Resources Defense Council in blocking Brazil from a $500m development loan until it dropped its plans to develop nuclear energy. All three countries, predictably, remain riddled with blackouts and energy scarcity thanks in part to the World Bank’s policies.

Since FDR’s American System-inspired policies of using credit to promote the general welfare were stymied by British meddling, it was Russia and China that stepped into the void.

The Soviet Union brought eight nuclear plants online in Finland, Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, Slovakia, Hungary, the GDR and almost Cuba. The Russian Federation and Rosatom completed projects in Iran, China, India, and ten other partner countries. China, with its Belt and Road Initiative, has or is constructing plants in Pakistan, Argentina and Kazakhstan, with plans underway in Saudi Arabia, Kenya, and Uzbekistan.

During that same time, the World Bank poured tens of billions of dollars into ineffective renewable energy projects around the world. Then-president Jim Yong Kim brashly stated “we don’t do nuclear energy” in 2013.

For the past two years Space Commune has been cataloguing these fissures in real time, from “Geopolitics Proving That Renewables Are for Show, Nuclear Is for Dough” to “RIP Anti-Nuclear Movement, Hello Anti-China Movement.” 

Our researched has showed that once Rosatom and CNNC proved they could deliver reactors on schedule, and once BRICS+ nations demanded 24/7 power to leap-frog into the industrial class, the West’s anti-nuclear taboo would collapse under its own contradictions.

As one energy analyst recently wrote: “If a village gets a solar energy unit that provides a few hours a day of power, this does not power machinery and stable supplies for refrigeration and water pumps. As a  result, this electricity access is highly limited in its ability to  spur economic growth, and it is incorrect to describe these villagers as having real access to electricity. Africans receiving a few hours a day of unreliable power should not be counted as achieving full electricity access.”

The World Bank’s about-face isn’t a revelation, it’s the endgame we predicted: an institution that spent decades funding weather-dependent gadgets finally forced to admit that high-density energy is the only route to real development.

This 2025 reversal does not erase that record, but it confirms what FDR assumed in 1944: prosperity, security and even peace ultimately rest on cheap, reliable, sovereign power. By returning to nuclear, however cautiously, the World Bank is inching back toward the mission it was built for.
